strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: applying system-theoretic tools (extended observability subspace, infinite Grassmannian geometry) to continual learning in SSMs is an interesting and underexplored angle, with a clear conceptual framing of why naive parameter/output regularization ignores SSM structure (P-equivalence, limited horizon).

Clean mathematical development: the derivation of the Gram matrix via the Sylvester equation (Lemma 5/10) is correct and self-contained, and the closed-form solution for diagonal A (Lemma 6/Eq. 17) is a nice, simple observation that makes the regularizer practical.

Broad and reasonably rigorous experimentation: three main benchmarks (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256), 5- and 10-task splits, three seeds with standard deviations, multiple CL metrics (AA, AIA, FM), plus integration with replay-based methods (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and prompt-based L2P, and ablations over the number of regularized blocks. Hyperparameters are fully disclosed in Appendix J.
Honest limitations section (Sec. 6) and a supplementary analysis (CKD on state matrices) that provides empirical grounding for design choices such as regularizing B in Inf-SSM+.
The method is simple (only two extra hyperparameters) and shown to be plug-and-play, which increases practical value.
weaknesses: Significant gap between the theoretical framework and what is actually implemented. The elegant infinite-Grassmannian chordal distance is ultimately replaced (Appendix D.5) by a rank-1 approximation with a heuristic discontinuity ('cos θ = 0 if ‖A−A′‖≤ε ∩ ‖C−C′‖≤ε'). The validation of this approximation is a synthetic Monte-Carlo simulation with Gaussian-sampled parameters, not analysis of real trained SSM states, so the headline claim of 'regularizing the infinite-horizon evolution' rests on an unvalidated-in-practice approximation.

The P-equivalence motivation is largely moot in practice: SSMs (S4D/Mamba/Vim) use a fixed diagonal parameterization, so the model never moves along the GL(n) orbit during training; invariance to reparameterization does not affect the actual optimization path. The core theoretical selling point thus contributes little to the empirical gains, which may largely come from generic, geometry-agnostic regularization of averaged state matrices.

The extension to S6/Mamba (§3.4) is a crude heuristic: averaging B and C over the outer dimension and applying soft-normalization departs substantially from the actual input-dependent, time-varying dynamics of selective SSMs, weakening the claim that the method regularizes the model's true long-term behavior.

Baselines are weak and dated. EFCIL comparisons are against EWC/SI/MAS/LwF only, while recent SOTA EFCIL methods (SSRE, LDC, EFC, and Mamba-specific CL methods like Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL discussed in the related work) are described but not compared. The large headline improvements (+29% AA, -33% FM in Fig. 1) are relative to old regularization baselines, and in the stronger replay setting (Table 2) results are mixed (e.g., LUCIR+Inf-SSM has lower AIA than LUCIR alone on ImageNet-R 5-task).

The O(n³)→O(n²) complexity 'contribution' is essentially trivial for diagonal A (element-wise reciprocal), and n=16 is tiny, so the FLOPS reduction is more of an implementation note than a substantive technical contribution; the appendix speed comparison (Table 8) is on synthetic random matrices.

Handling of B (controllability) remains unsolved: Inf-SSM+ uses a plain Frobenius norm, which the authors themselves admit is not orbit-invariant, and the CKD analysis (§H.1) is inconclusive about whether B regularization matters.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is stated despite detailed hyperparameters; the 'scan-breaking' implementation (Appendix E) that re-extracts intermediate states outside the CUDA kernel introduces training-time/VRAM costs that are acknowledged but not quantified.

Presentation issues: inconsistent naming (EwC/EWC, LwF-AC in Table 1 vs. LwF-MC in text; LwF-ABC appears only in appendix), typos ('B~i,j' subscripting in Eq. 36, 'CA′2' in Theorem 9's matrix), and the appendix lemmas on distance equivalence (Appendix I) are only local (θ→0) results of limited relevance.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely underexplored problem: equipping State-Space Models (SSMs) with exemplar-free continual learning. Framing forgetting through the lens of system theory (P-equivalence, extended observability subspace, infinite-dimensional Grassmannian) is a novel and intellectually interesting perspective that goes beyond standard weight-space regularization.

The core mathematical derivation is largely sound: the reduction of the cross-Gram matrix computation to a Sylvester equation (Lemma 5/10), and the closed-form Hadamard-division solution when A is diagonal (Lemma 6), are correct and self-contained. Proofs of P-equivalence invariance (Appendix C) are included and check out.

The evaluation breadth is respectable: three datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) plus CUB-200 for ablations, 5- and 10-task splits, three seeds with standard deviations, and integration with replay-based methods (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and prompt-based methods (L2P-R) to demonstrate modularity.

The paper is honest about several limitations, including the lack of P-equivalence invariance in Inf-SSM+, the 'scan-breaking' training overhead, and the trade-off introduced by the B-regularization term. The ablations on CKD analysis and number of regularized blocks add useful insight.
Hyperparameters for all methods, seeds, and hardware are reported in detail (Appendix J), which supports reproducibility of the experimental protocol.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the theoretical framing and what is actually implemented. The elegant infinite-horizon Grassmannian machinery is ultimately replaced in practice by a crude rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix (Appendix D.5), validated only by a synthetic Monte-Carlo simulation on randomly sampled matrices, not on real trained Vim models. The 'cos θ = 0 if A ≈ A′' patch is an ad hoc fix that further undercuts the geometric story. The actual loss used in experiments is far simpler than the theory suggests, and the paper does not adequately confront this.

The central ablation supporting the paper's core claim is missing: a direct comparison between the proposed Grassmannian/observability distance and a naive Frobenius-norm regularization of (A, C) under identical settings. Without this, it is impossible to verify that the sophisticated geometry-aware formulation—rather than simply regularizing the state parameters—drives the reported gains. The paper regularizes B with a plain Frobenius norm in Inf-SSM+, so the baseline was trivial to include.

The baselines are weak and outdated. The main EFCIL comparison (Table 1) is against EWC, SI, MAS, and LwF, all from 2017–2018. Modern EFCIL methods (SSRE, LDC, EFC) are discussed in Appendix F but never compared against, and no explanation is given beyond complexity concerns. The headline claim of 'significant outperformance' is therefore not established against the current state of the art, and the re-implemented baselines restricted to (A, C) in Table 1 raise fairness questions despite the appendix experiment.

The computational contribution is oversold. The O(n³)→O(n²) reduction applies only because A is diagonal, for which the closed-form solution is a trivial element-wise division; the authors themselves note that O(n³) is 'quite affordable' at n=16. Absolute wall-clock costs, including the acknowledged 'scan-breaking' overhead (recomputing and saving intermediate states), are never reported, so the practical efficiency claims (e.g., '100× FLOPS reduction') are not substantiated end-to-end.

Internal inconsistencies and reporting errors undermine confidence: the replay-integration improvement is stated as 'reduces FM by 38.41% in 5-task and 41.89% in 10-task' in §5.1 but as '6.66% FM reduction' in Appendix G.4 for the same experiment; percentages vs. percentage points are conflated throughout (e.g., 'improves AA by 29.21%' for a gain from 33.92 to 43.82); the ablation in Table 7 shows FM increasing as more blocks are regularized, which contradicts the stability narrative and is explained only hand-wavily.

The method is evaluated on a single backbone (Vim-small) and only on image classification, despite the paper's framing around SSMs as general sequence models. No experiments on other SSM variants (Mamba, Mamba-2) or sequence tasks are provided, limiting the claimed generality of the approach.

Presentation issues are non-trivial: notation and reference errors (e.g., 'Theorem 10' cited in D.3 for a result stated as Lemma 10/Theorem 9; inconsistent naming L_ISM vs. L_I_SM vs. 'ISM'), typos ('both method leads'), and a main-text narrative (Eq. 15, three Sylvester equations) that diverges from the actual simplified distance (Eq. 38) used in practice, requiring careful cross-referencing to determine what was really computed.
No code release is mentioned, which—combined with the deviation between described and implemented methods—makes independent verification of the results difficult.

strengths: Novel and interesting research direction: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to formulate exemplar-free continual learning for SSMs through the geometry of the extended observability subspace on the infinite Grassmannian, rather than constraining weights directly. The P-equivalence argument (Definition 2, Theorem 4) is a well-grounded observation from system theory that motivates the approach.

The core derivation is clean and correct: the Gram matrix G = sum_t (A^T)^t C^T C' (A')^t satisfying the Sylvester equation A^T G A' - G = -C^T C' (Lemma 5/10) is a neat reduction, and the closed-form element-wise solution when A is diagonal (Lemma 6/17) is valid and clearly derived.

Comprehensive empirical support: three datasets (ImageNet-R, CIFAR-100, Caltech-256) plus CUB for ablations, 5- and 10-task splits, three seeds with std, integration with replay-based (ER, LUCIR, X-DER) and prompt-based (L2P-R) methods, block-count ablations (Tab. 7), CKD analysis of state drift (Figs. 3-4), timing comparisons (Tab. 8), and full hyperparameter tables (Tabs. 9-12). Reproducibility is well supported.

Fair experimental design in several places: the authors explicitly acknowledge when Inf-SSM is disadvantaged (regularizing only (A,C) while baselines regularize (A,B,C), Tab. 4/5) and report settings where the method loses (LUCIR+Inf-SSM on ImageNet-R 5-task, Tab. 2), which increases credibility.
Honest limitations section: the lack of controllability (B) regularization in the invariant loss, the extra hyperparameter in Inf-SSM+, and the loss of orbit invariance are candidly stated.
weaknesses: Gap between the headline theory and the implemented method. The main text (Sec. 3.3, 3.5, Eq. 15/18) develops the full chordal distance on the infinite Grassmannian via three Sylvester equations, but Appendix D.5 reveals the actual loss uses a rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix with cos^2 theta = Tr(G3G4)/Tr(G1)Tr(G2). This surrogate is validated only by a Monte Carlo simulation with Gaussian-sampled parameters (Pearson r = -0.8962), not on the real trained Vim states, and it is not a proper metric (cos theta != 1 even when O1 = O2, patched by an ad-hoc epsilon check). The framing overstates the theoretical rigor of what is actually deployed.

The O(n^3) to O(n^2) claim is technically true but somewhat trivial: when A is diagonal, the Sylvester equation is element-wise decoupled and admits a closed form by construction; no sophisticated structure is being exploited. With n = 16 (the actual Vim setting), the absolute FLOPS savings are negligible relative to a 40-epoch training run of a full backbone, making the '100x FLOPS reduction' contribution largely cosmetic.

The extension to selective SSMs (S6/Mamba/Vim) is heuristic: averaging the state parameters over the outer dimension o, treating each sequence position tau as an independent LTI trajectory, and applying Soft-Normalization for Schur stability are approximations whose fidelity for input-dependent Mamba parameters is not analyzed. The theory strictly applies to LTI systems, and the paper does not quantify how far the actual model deviates from this assumption.

Baseline strength is limited. The main EFCIL comparisons are against EwC, SI, MAS, and LwF - methods from 2017-2018 - while modern hybrid EFCIL methods (SSRE, LDC, EFC) are discussed in Appendix F but not compared. Absolute accuracies are also low (AA ~43.8% on ImageNet-R 10-task), making cross-paper comparison difficult. Replay experiments are more informative but mixed (Inf-SSM sometimes reduces AIA for LUCIR).

The ablation in Tab. 7 contradicts the method's premise: FM is lowest when regularizing only the final block (23.18 on ImageNet-R; 1.19 on CUB) and increases when regularizing all 24 blocks (36.34; 45.88), which the authors themselves flag as unexpected. The offered explanation (overfitting to the regularization loss in fewer layers reducing plasticity) is speculative and not experimentally validated.

The claim of not relying on 'information from prior tasks' needs qualification: Inf-SSM requires storing a full copy of the previous task's model, which is parameter-level information from prior tasks; the paper should be clearer that the advantage is only over exemplar/feature storage.

Presentation issues: notation inconsistencies (O_infty row vs. column convention flipped between main text Eq. 10 and Appendix D.3/D.4; the Sylvester equation sign/transposed forms differ between Lemma 5, Appendix C.3, and D.4), and Appendix I's local equivalence of Grassmannian distances is a marginal result of limited value. No code release is mentioned.

strengths: Novel and underexplored direction: the paper is among the first to address continual learning for state-space models by exploiting SSM-specific structure (extended observability subspace, P-equivalence invariance) rather than treating SSMs as generic networks. This is a genuinely fresh angle relative to existing CL work on MLPs/CNNs/Transformers.

Principled mathematical formulation: the derivation of chordal distance on the infinite Grassmannian via a Gram/Sylvester equation (Lemma 4/9) is clean, the proofs in the appendix are self-contained, and the O(n^3)->O(n^2) closed-form solution for diagonal A (Lemma 5) is a correct and practically useful simplification.

Broad empirical validation: the method is integrated into five diverse CIL baselines (ER, LUCIR, X-DER, L2P-R, CLFD) and compared against EFCIL methods (EWC, SI, MAS, LwF variants, plus UCL in the appendix) across three datasets, two task counts, and three seeds. Consistent gains (avg +8.31% AA, -9.36% FM) with larger improvements as task count grows support the plug-and-play claim.

Additional analyses strengthen the case: latency comparison vs. EWC/X-DER (Table 3), ablations on number of regularized blocks, CKA/CKD analysis of state drift across layers, Inf-SSM+ variant testing the role of B, and Vim-tiny results all address natural follow-up questions.

Reproducibility is well supported: full hyperparameter tables for every dataset/task-count/method combination, backbone, seeds, and hardware are reported in the appendix; the algorithm is given explicitly, and the diagonal-A restriction is honestly acknowledged in the limitations with a general-A fallback (Theorem 10).
weaknesses: Gap between theory and implementation: while the theory covers general LTI SSMs, the actual method relies on two non-trivial approximations for modern selective SSMs: (i) averaging the time-varying A_t over the sequence (justified only by variance statistics in Table 5, where preserved variance of 0.0315 for the outer dimension is quite low), and (ii) a rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix (Appendix D.5) validated only by a Monte Carlo correlation of -0.896 with a noise surrogate, plus an ad-hoc epsilon patch to handle cos(theta)=1 when O1=O2. These heuristics weaken the 'geometry-faithful' narrative.

Limited backbone scope: all main experiments use Vim-small only (Vim-tiny in the appendix). No results on Mamba, Mamba-2, or VMamba, which are the architectures the theory for selective SSMs (Section 3.3) is ostensibly designed for, so the generality claims are not empirically tested beyond one model family.

Comparison fairness and baseline strength: Table 2 deliberately places EFCIL baselines at a disadvantage (regularizing (A,B,C) vs. Inf-SSM's (A,C)); although Table 6 and the UCL comparison mitigate this, the primary presentation could mislead. The EFCIL baseline set (EWC/SI/MAS/LwF) is largely pre-2018, and none of the Mamba-specific CL methods (Mamba-CL, MambaCL, Mamba-FSCIL) are empirically compared, with the exclusion justified mainly on scope grounds.

Accuracy gains over integrated baselines are sometimes marginal and AIA occasionally decreases (e.g., LUCIR 5-task ImageNet-R), suggesting the main benefit is reduced forgetting rather than better plasticity, which the paper does acknowledge but does not deeply analyze.

The headline O(n^3)->O(n^2) and 100x FLOPS reduction, while correct, is of limited practical significance for n=16 (Sylvester solves were already 'quite affordable' per the authors' own appendix), and the separate rank-1 distance (Eq. 33) used in practice means the carefully derived Gram-matrix machinery is largely bypassed at runtime.

Some presentation issues: the two experiment tracks (parameter regularization vs. full state regularization) with different baseline configurations are confusing to follow; notation switches between A-bar and A mid-paper; and no code release link is mentioned despite detailed hyperparameters.

strengths: The paper targets a genuinely under-explored problem: continual learning specifically tailored to the geometry of state-space models, and the extended-observability/Grassmannian framing is an interesting and fresh angle relative to generic weight-regularization methods like EWC/SI/MAS.

The core derivations are largely sound: the closed-form Gram matrix via the Sylvester equation (Lemma 4/9) is correct, and the element-wise solution for diagonal A (Eq. 14) is valid, with proofs of P-equivalence and subspace invariance provided for self-containment.

The empirical program is broad: Inf-SSM is integrated into five CIL baselines (ER, LUCIR, X-DER, L2P-R, CLFD) across three datasets and two task splits, plus isolated EFCIL comparisons (including a re-implemented UCL), latency measurements, layer ablations, and a Vim-tiny validation. FM reductions are consistent across settings.

Reproducibility support is strong: hyperparameters for every dataset/baseline/task-split are fully tabulated (Tables 12-19), multiple seeds are reported with standard deviations, and implementation caveats (e.g., the scan-breaking limitation) are honestly disclosed.
weaknesses: There is a substantial gap between the headline theory and what is actually used. The main paper advertises distances on an 'infinite-dimensional Grassmannian' computed via chordal distance with three Sylvester equations, but Appendix D.5 reveals the implemented loss is a heavily simplified rank-1 trace formula (Eq. 33), validated only by a Monte-Carlo simulation under synthetic Gaussian assumptions. In practice the method reduces to a normalized similarity of (A, C), which weakens the claimed geometric contribution and the novelty narrative.

The celebrated O(n^3) to O(n^2) speedup is trivial: for diagonal A, the Sylvester equation decouples element-wise and Eq. 14 is just an element-wise division. With n=16 in Vim-small, this is a minor engineering observation rather than a contribution, and the '100x FLOPS reduction' framing overstates its significance.

The extension to selective SSMs (Section 3.3) is heuristic: averaging the A matrices over the outer dimension and applying soft-normalization to force Schur stability means the regularized object is no longer the actual SSM dynamics of the model being trained. This approximation is justified only by a variance-preservation statistic (Table 5) on one dataset.

Evidence quality concerns: Table 1 explicitly states baselines 'cannot be directly compared' due to differing batch sizes and epochs, which undermines the headline integration gains in Fig. 1. Per-batch latency for Inf-SSM (0.096s) is 10x that of EWC (0.0095s), yet the text claims being 'on par with simple CL methods.' The ablation in Table 7 shows FM worsening as more blocks are regularized, with a strained explanation that conflicts with the paper's stability claims.

The comparison set for the EFCIL 'isolation test' is dated (EWC, SI, MAS, LwF from 2017-2018); recent strong exemplar-free methods (e.g., EFC, LDC, SSRE) are discussed but excluded by fiat, and no Transformer backbone is evaluated under the same budget to show the gains are SSM-specific rather than simply a strong distillation-style regularizer.

Absolute performance is weak in several cells (e.g., AA of 26.5% on CIFAR-100 10-task; ER improvements of under 1%), and the claimed Theorem 3 is acknowledged by the authors to be a well-known result from system identification, so the theoretical novelty rests almost entirely on the (trivial) diagonal shortcut.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: the paper is, to my knowledge, the first to formulate exemplar-free continual learning directly in terms of the state-space geometry of SSMs (extended observability subspace on the infinite Grassmannian), rather than treating SSM parameters as generic weights. This is a genuinely fresh angle in the CL literature.

Solid and self-contained theoretical development: P-equivalence (Definition 1), invariance of the observability subspace under P-equivalence (Theorem 3, proof in App. C.2), and the Sylvester-equation formulation for the Gram matrix (Lemma 4/9) are correct and well-presented. The reduction from O(n^3) to O(n^2) for diagonal A (Lemma 5, App. D.4) is clean and validated by a latency study (Table 3).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: integration with five diverse CL methods (ER, LUCIR, X-DER, L2P-R, CLFD) across three datasets and 5/10-task splits (Table 1), an isolation study against EFCIL baselines where baselines are given a deliberately favorable setup (regularizing A,B,C vs. Inf-SSM's A,C only; Table 2), an additional recent baseline UCL (Table 11), Vim-tiny results (Table 10), ablations on the number of regularized blocks (Table 7), a distance-metric speed comparison (Table 8), and a B-regularization variant (Inf-SSM+) that supports the claim that regularizing A,C suffices (Table 9).

Reproducibility is strong: complete hyperparameter tables for every dataset/setting (Tables 12-19), three seeds with standard deviations, and detailed algorithmic description (Algorithm 1), including honest disclosure of implementation limitations (state-breaking hack in App. E).

Consistent and sizable gains: average +8.31% AA and -9.36% FM when integrated into existing methods, with larger gains in the harder 10-task setting, which supports the claim that the method captures state evolution over long task sequences.
weaknesses: The gap between theory and the practical method is larger than the presentation suggests. The clean LTI/Grassmannian theory applies to fixed (A,C); for selective SSMs (Mamba/Vim), the method relies on approximations: averaging A_t over the outer dimension with variance justification by Table 5 (mean variance preserved only 0.0315 with high std), and soft-normalization to enforce Schur stability. These are reasonable engineering choices but weaken the claim that the method regularizes 'the' infinite-horizon behavior of the deployed architecture.

The rank-1 approximation of the observability matrix and the simplified distance (App. D.5) is ad hoc. The Monte-Carlo validation uses randomly sampled Gaussian matrices, which may not reflect trained networks; the patch 'cos(theta)=1 if parameters changed by less than epsilon' is a heuristic discontinuity in the loss. The authors show it works empirically (Table 9, H.3), but the theoretical framing overstates how principled the deployed objective is.

The headline theoretical result (invariance of the observability subspace under P-equivalence) is acknowledged by the authors to be well known in system identification (citing [27]). The novelty is therefore primarily in the application and computational machinery rather than in the theory itself, which should be stated more prominently.

Baselines in the EFCIL comparison (EWC, SI, MAS, LwF) are classical; the isolation study would be more convincing with stronger recent EFCIL methods beyond UCL (e.g., SSRE, LDC, EFC, which are discussed in App. F but not compared). The claim that such methods are excluded due to architectural incompatibility is plausible but not empirically demonstrated.

The note that baseline numbers 'cannot be directly compared' across methods due to differing batch sizes/epochs (Table 1) is unusual and could mask favorable tuning of the proposed method; the extensive per-method hyperparameter tables mitigate but do not fully remove this concern.

Absolute accuracies are modest (e.g., ~43% AA on ImageNet-R 10-task), and the ablation showing FM increasing with more regularized blocks (Table 7) is counterintuitive and only partially explained, suggesting the stability-plasticity trade-off of the method is not fully characterized.
